entries.title: These are the gifts developers will actually want
entries.summary: The developer you're shopping for hasn’t shared their holiday wish list with you yet? Check out these gifts, plus our Black Friday discount all week long. The post These are the gifts developers will actually want appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
The developer you’re shopping for hasn’t shared their holiday wish list with you yet? Check out these gifts, plus our Black Friday discount all week long.

Some people tell you exactly what they want for the holidays, but some people just don’t. The gifts, the decor, the food, for all of it, you have to guess at what they might like. You trawl thousands of gift guide lists titled “the definitive gift guide for 2026,” but none of the guides are quite right for that special person. That is, until this one came along.

As long as that person in your life is a developer.

We won’t say it’s the definitive guide for the developer in your life (or for yourself, we won’t judge), but we have brought together a few of our favorite pieces from the GitHub Shop for you to pick from.

Get building

At GitHub Universe this year we brought our brand new GitHub x Omnitype Bauer Lite Keyboard Kit to the Makerspace for our attendees to build. To say it was popular is an understatement. If you like building keyboards, you’ll want the details. Each GitHub-exclusive Bauer Lite kit arrives in a randomly selected color combination and includes a hot-swap PCB with RGB underglow, Omnitype Hawk linear switches, dye-sublimated PBT keycaps, and the essential hardware and tools for a hands-on custom build. And if you’re new to building keyboards then you can follow along with our step-by-step guide.

If you like building of a different variety, perhaps our new GitHub jigsaw puzzle will be calling you. Grab yourself a hot beverage, settle in, and start building. Speaking of which…

Get cozy

If the preference is to work on the sofa in ultimate comfort, then this is the gift guide for you. Drape a cozy blanket over you, put on some warm socks, and while your agent is busy at work you can slip on the sleep mask and have a little mid-afternoon nap.

Get decorating

If the desk of you or your loved one is looking a bit dull, brighten it up with a colorful desk mat, selection of mugs and tumblers, and two buddies to help with all your coding decisions. The Copilot Amazeball sits on your desk until you have a burning question. Should you ship on a Friday? Give the Amazeball a shake, turn it over, and get your answer. Your other tiny teammate, the Mona Octobobble, will simply nod along to all your best ideas. Of which, we’re certain, there are many.

Get traveling

If your January resolution is to become a digital nomad then there are gifts here for you, too, especially if you have all the ideas but no gear. From tech organizers to work totes to awesome skateboards, we’ll get you where you need to go in style.

Super fans unite

Super fans, check out some of our most popular items from the shop, like our classic invertocat hoodie. Plus get your hands on the matching version for your drink.

Cold outside? Then dress up your outfit with our Mona Varsity jacket. Too warm for that? Then you’ll love our Cabana shirt and shorts co-ord.

Something for the next generation

Whether it’s for a brand-new baby or the tweenager just getting into coding, we have something for all ages. Start them off with the Invertocat onesie and move on into the matching Mona bestie bottle and Mona plush.

Shipping fees? 404 Not Found.

We have a special Black Friday deal for you: Use code FREESHIPBLOG26 for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026 and ensure your gifts arrive by December 22 by checking out our holiday shipping deadlines. Happy shopping!

entries.title: The best things in open source are built together
entries.summary: Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion. The post The best things in open source are built together appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion.

In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities.

Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine.

Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework.

I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed.

This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked:

“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”

John replied:

“I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.”

Replica, a new open-source design harness

In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit.

GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground

John Maeda, CVP GitHub & CoreAI Design

With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate.

With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit.

A11y Framework, a new open-source accessibility framework

Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all.

As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer.

Ed Summers, GitHub Head of Accessibility

The Open Source Accessibility Framework, created in collaboration with external contributors from the disability and accessibility communities, launched last month. It helps make accessibility an inherent part of how projects are created. It is an accountability model with four phases so developers can turn projects and accessibility goals into public, trackable progress. A core component of this is the new 

ACCESSIBILITY.md
file, a file now visible on repository overview pages, giving a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. Read more about the 
ACCESSIBILITY.md
file.

The power of community

Going back to John and Qianqian’s Universe talk, John asked:

“How does an open source community keep something lasting that long? What’s the secret?”

Qianqian replied:

“I think the secret is one of the most obvious ones. Community.”

The GitHub repo firstcontributions/first-contributions ranked fourth among the fastest-growing community projects in 2026 by contributors, helping developers take their first steps into open source. We hope you can join our open-source community: hack away at our new projects or start your own.

Watch John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session 👇

entries.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
entries.summary: In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects. Maintainers have already fixed more than half. The post Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes. appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects. Maintainers have already fixed more than half.

AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings.

AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings?

GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH, Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on.

The process

Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked:

  1. Find. Codename MDASH, an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found.
  2. Filter. An AI triage agent from the GitHub Security Lab, built on tailored Copilot skills, removed duplicates, checked validity, and focused on high-impact bugs, so maintainers never had to review raw scan results.
  3. Report privately. Reports reached maintainers through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, with a proof of concept and a suggested fix.
  4. Fix. Maintainers decided what to fix, how to fix it, and when.

Reports and fixes stayed on GitHub, where maintainers already work.

The result: Codename MDASH, using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues across the six projects. After AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports. As of November 15, they had fixed 55, and 14 of those fixes were already in a release.

What we learned

These lessons come from what the six projects fixed and what their maintainers chose to share. Six projects is a small sample, so read them as early lessons.

1. Fixes matter more than findings

Fixing is where maintainers spend their time. So every report arrived already checked, with a suggested fix to review, adapt, and merge. Maintainers started from a well-scoped patch, not a raw finding.

The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of the reports they received in a week or less. Maintainers used the suggested fixes, some as written and some with changes.

AutoGPT’s maintainers had recently shipped a new check, and it was broken. The report landed three days later and pointed at the right line. They took the fix further than the suggested patch, wrote it within a day, and had it in production less than a week later.

Finding vulnerabilities is no longer our bottleneck. Fixing them is the hard part, and that depends on maintainers.
Netty maintainer

2. Codename MDASH, with researcher review, gave maintainers high-quality findings with fixes

Maintainers got a short list, not a flood. Express maintainers said the reports cut through the noise. Caddy maintainers said they surfaced obscure bugs and filled gaps that earlier reports had missed. For FastMCP, the scan went beyond what AI scanners had given them before. ImageMagick, maintained by a two-person team, received 22 reports.

AI did the finding, researchers did the checking, and maintainers stayed in charge.

One ImageMagick report looked like a kind of issue the maintainers had seen before. Its summary showed it wasn’t and pointed to the exact lines of code. They were able to push a fix in 15 minutes.

Normally, a security advisory would take us around 30 minutes to 1 hour on average to read, understand, and make a fix. It is a huge difference.
ImageMagick maintainer
Codename MDASH was able to find unknown, obscure security bugs in our project with succinct reports, and it filled in gaps from some prior reports that hadn’t been noticed.
Caddy maintainer

3. Open source still has gaps to close

The pilot worked because people did careful work at every step, and that work doesn’t scale yet. Seven researchers spent about two days per project checking findings by hand. Meanwhile, low-quality reports still reach maintainers every day.

For open source, fixes need to be delivered via private vulnerability reporting (PVR). Maintainers need to run CI/CD tests on private forks to verify those fixes. And to close the gap between defenders and attackers, maintainers need access to cyber-capable models to verify a proof of concept, before and after the fix.

The Codename MDASH scan provided unique insights into the security of our project above and beyond what AI scanners have provided us in the past
FastMCP maintainer

Why it matters

If you’re a maintainer, this approach changes what a security report costs you. A checked, private report that comes with a suggested fix takes less of your time. You shouldn’t have to triage a scanner’s output. That’s the sender’s job.

If you use AI to find vulnerabilities in open source, maintainers’ feedback points to this standard:

  • Check every finding before you send it, against what the project already knows and against its threat model and security policy.
  • Report it privately.
  • Include a suggested fix. Let maintainers set the pace.
Features are easier and easier to ship, but in the future maintaining software will probably come down to who cares enough to manage the security.
AutoGPT maintainer
Codename MDASH is very useful for cutting through the noise of vulnerability reports.
Express maintainer

What you can do today

  • If you maintain any open source project, turn on private vulnerability reporting so researchers can report security issues to you without making them public. If your project is on GitHub, turn on core security features in about two minutes with 
    gh-secure
    .
  • If you build on open source, turn on Dependabot alerts so you know when a dependency you use needs a security update.
  • If you send AI-generated vulnerability reports to open source projects, hold them to the standard above before you send them.
  • Repositories using GitHub code security can use agentic autofix to help automatically remediate their alerts with Copilot

What happens next

  1. Fixes, where maintainers already work. GitHub is bringing these lessons into private vulnerability reporting and security advisories, where GitHub Security Lab is already investing to reduce the burden of low-quality reports on maintainers.
  2. MAI Cyber 2. Today Microsoft announced MAI Cyber 2. The Codename MDASH pilot ran on the earlier MAI Cyber model. GitHub and Microsoft will keep working together to help secure open source.
  3. Closing the gaps, starting with the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund. We’re working with Microsoft to scale researcher review without cutting corners. GitHub will offer every alumni project AI security scans, with findings checked before they’re reported privately. Alumni also get GitHub Copilot Max. We’ll bring this support to future sessions of the Fund.

Everyone downstream benefits from this system. When a maintainer publishes a security advisory on GitHub and it’s reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can alert the repositories that depend on that package. That’s the idea behind the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund: 216 projects so far, with more than 300 maintainers fixing more than 4,000 vulnerabilities in software downloaded more than 20 billion times a month.

Thank you

To the maintainers of AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty: thank you for your time, your trust, and your feedback. Thank you also to the Codename MDASH team at Microsoft Security, the MAI Cyber team, the researchers of Microsoft FORGE Lab, and GitHub Security Lab.

Maintainers do the fixing. Our job is to make sure they never do it alone.

Hear from maintainers about their experience with Codename MDASH. 👇

About the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund

All six projects in this pilot are alumni of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, which gives each project $10,000 through GitHub Sponsors, plus security training and a supportive alumni community.

The GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, powered by GitHub Sponsors, funds open source projects that underpin the digital supply chain, catalyze innovation, and are critical to the AI stack. Want your company to help secure the open source it depends on? Become a funding partner through the Fund page. Learn more about the Fund or apply.

Through the Fund, maintainers receive security training and Azure credits from Microsoft for Startups. That support sits alongside Microsoft’s European Security Program and its Secure Future Initiative, whose principle is security above all else. Most organizations are downstream in the same way. If your software depends on open source, do the same: back the maintainers you rely on.

I work on open source strategy and programs that support maintainers inside GitHub and across the ecosystem. I also serve on the Steering Committee for the TODO Group, where we help organizations use and sustain open source responsibly.

entries.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
entries.summary: Discover how we built the open Agent Host Protocol to keep your agent sessions accessible across editors, apps, phones, and the cloud. The post Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
Discover how we built the open Agent Host Protocol to keep your agent sessions accessible across editors, apps, phones, and the cloud.

Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices.

In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows.

Why one integration per client stopped working

GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have.

At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity.

Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but developers also still want to be able to pull their agents into their own workflows–whether that’s an editor, a terminal, a phone, or a tool they built themselves–and they can’t do that if every client needs its own one-off integration. That’s why developers needed a protocol: a standard, independently versioned language across versions of VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, mobile apps, and any other client that might host an agent. A shared protocol means every client sees the same agents, history, and state without bespoke integrations, and you aren’t tied to one app’s idea of what an agent session is.

Designing a protocol for agents on every client

The protocol needed to allow multiple clients to interact with the same set of agents seamlessly. Start a session in the cloud from your phone, for example, then continue it from your laptop. It should tolerate network interruptions, reconnections, and concurrent client mutations. And it needed to be full-featured enough for you to do real work from each of your clients.

At the same time, the protocol needed to stay out of agent behavior. Unlike the domains that produced the Language Server Protocol and Debug Adapter Protocol, the world of agents is evolving quickly. That’s why AHP avoids encoding how agents work, and instead focuses on how you want to interact with them.

You also need the protocol to be simple enough to implement on your own client or server. While the full feature set would necessarily be extensive, the core protocol needed to be minimal.

The result of these requirements is the Agent Host Protocol (AHP). It is oriented around URI-identified “channels”, which are the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, but can also implement more channels that provide terminal support, MCP additions, or OTel reporting, for example.

Within each channel is a reducer-based state object, which drives most of the logic for clients. The server is the arbiter of the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects, like sending a chat message. This provides a few very nice properties. Reconnection and replay in poor network conditions are easy: a client sends all queued actions, presents the right ‘loading’ state, and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions before confirming them. Clients and servers are straightforward to debug. And reducer-based state also plays nicely with popular UI frameworks like React.

Shipping five clients and two hosts

Adopting the Agent Host Protocol in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The Copilot Chat extension, which used to provide all of VS Code’s AI and agentic capabilities, had been growing for over three years, reaching over 400,000 lines of TypeScript, not counting tests. But, as a VS Code extension, it was structured around the lifecycle of a VS Code window and depended entirely on the VS Code extension API. Neither that lifetime nor those APIs would be available in a standalone agent host process.

As we started building the Agent Host Protocol in early 2026, the Copilot SDK was also being developed, and it made sense to leverage it as the foundation for the new agentic stack. This was a big transition. It’s easy to build a harness implementation that says hello and can edit files—we were using the agent host to develop the agent host after the first couple weeks—but it’s another thing to build one that covers the long tail of features developers had come to expect from Copilot Chat.

GitHub has had Copilot cloud agents for a couple of years, allowing developers to run tasks in the cloud from any device. While VS Code was quietly developing the Agent Host Protocol, GitHub was looking to expand that capability to coordinate sessions running on your own devices via the Copilot app, or in cloud sandboxes. This was exactly the 

N:M
problem that AHP was built to solve, so adopting the same technology made perfect sense.

From the outset, the GitHub Agent Host had different requirements than VS Code’s implementation. VS Code runs the host locally and can drop its host on other compute over SSH, containers, WSL, or Dev Tunnels, and it is actually included as part of the VS Code Server bundle. The GitHub Agent Host needed to run in the cloud and across a much wider variety of infrastructure, environments, and security constraints.

Those differing requirements are why they’re separate implementations written in different languages: VS Code’s in TypeScript and GitHub’s in Rust. For now, having two agent hosts has been a good acid-test for the protocol itself. How well does it work when two entirely different teams and sets of agents implement the same protocol independently?

Pretty well, it turns out. Like MCP, the Agent Host Protocol provides escape hatches via custom methods and 

_meta
data on objects that consumers can use for out-of-band signaling. After several months heads-down on our respective implementations, our first task as we worked toward unification was inventorying the ways each implementation had extended the protocol. Many of these extensions reasonably stay GitHub-specific, such as the GitHub Agent Host using metadata to link to project boards. In other cases, variance was a sign of a gap in the protocol; early versions, for example, could not accurately represent shell-type tool output that wasn’t backed by a PTY. And some were bad assumptions, like VS Code’s client assuming a particular structure for the session URIs it received from the agent host. A protocol with only one implementation isn’t truly portable; as we taught our clients and servers to talk to each other, AHP became portable in practice, not just in theory.

Today, the Agent Host Protocol provides that same continuity across all VS Code and GitHub surfaces. Agent sessions running locally in the GitHub Copilot app, in cloud sandboxes, and in VS Code all share the same underlying protocol. To see how it’s used, read about how you can work from anywhere with the new connected Copilot cloud experience.

Using the Agent Host Protocol

AHP was designed to be easy to use in clients and servers. Agent Host Protocol libraries are available in Rust, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, .NET, and Go, and agents are able to build clients and servers with little prompting. I have a macropad sitting on my desk that reflects my agent’s state in real time, and others have built everything from smart watch apps to Kanban-style task management tools against the protocol. Whether you want a companion app for your own agents, a way to bring agent sessions into your team’s tools, or AHP support in your own editor or agent, the protocol is open for you to build on.

You can connect to an agent host you implement in the Copilot app (enable Experimental > Direct Connections, then go to Environments > Add Agent Host Protocol Host) and in VS Code (via Add Remote Agent Host in the Agents window). You can spawn a standalone version of VS Code’s agent host by running 

code agent host
in your terminal, or see the endpoints for the one in your editor by running 
code agent endpoints
, and samples can help you and your agent get started.

The Agent Host Protocol is an open standard, and questions and suggestions are welcome on GitHub.

Happy coding!
